title: Pete Lala's, learning trombone from Vic Gaspard, and Armstrong in the brass band
summary: Red-light district work, then taking up trombone with Vic Gaspard, a first brass band job with Remus, and Louis Armstrong's cramps.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Beverly Garden. That's Beverly Garden. So we had mean old man, Kimball and all of us. Papa Celestine, he went with Rizzley too. And we left Hampton Benson, I originally being a trauma player at South. And T.O., he quit P-Rone, he went on over there with us too. So we stuck out there and- You played drums then? He stuck out there a long time, making good money. So well, the boys got to say they want to go back to the red light. Went on back to the red light and played at King Holler. King Holler was at Pete Lawler's playing there with Mac and Mac and their Mac Mac show. At King Holler, Buddy Krishna on piano, Omer Valtu on violin. The band in them days didn't have a violin. Didn't have no leader. A lot of them was leaning. Henry Zeno on drum. I remember that. No bass. While the floor show was going pretty good. And one night, we goes through there and Henry Zeno laid off. He didn't lay off the standing time. I said, come on, rest me up man. So he went to gambling. He never did come back. So that's when Joe started to organ with Mary. Mary Mac and Mac. He said, that's my homeboy. We all from our years. We all was sticking together, playing together. We got along. So Henry come on back. So they fired Henry for me. At least I knew Henry was a first class drummer, but I was a younger man than Henry. That's all. So Mac said, well we going to make a trip. Will you come with us? I said, I don't mind. I said, but I'm learning how to play trombone now. I'm going to play trombone. She said, sure. I said, what's the idea? I said, well old man Piku and I was going out to West End there one night. He said, man, you a young man. Why don't you learn how to play something before you get to a low, them drums all around. I said, I take no peak. We used to call him peak. Pike. I take Pike's advice. I pick up the trombone. I started to pull around with the trombone. I said, well I'm going to Vic Gasper. So Vic was one of the greatest baritone players and trombone players in the city of New Orleans. I said, will you teach me a pop? He said, sure. Come on. Come on. Asked Creole. I went to Vic's house. He bought me a catechism. Not a catechism. Imperial record. Method. With no horn. So he took me over to Method and I called All I Know So Good. I didn't know much of bass clip music but I knew plenty of treble clipped because I used to play bells with my drums. Oh, yeah, sure. So I went over to bass clip music and two weeks after he told me, get your horn pops. That's all you need is a horn. That's all right. That's all. I went over there and I said my friend Harrison Barnes. I said, Harry, I'm going to learn how to play trombone. I learned how to your horn. He said, I got a whole horn, yeah. I said, it'll slide in much. So you can have the bells. I come on up to town, you're ready to play old Jack Carey at his barbershop. I said, Jack, you got an old trombone on the line, play trombone. He said, yeah, take both or take yours. There's one, take one. So Jack's slide was good but I used the Harrison Barnes bell and Jack's slide, put it together. I went to Vic Gasper house. I run through the method so quick. In two weeks time, Vic told me, leave the book home, pops. Well, I left the book home and he had some of his orchestration music with John Robeshow and him using the brass in the orchestra. Went over to music. He said, oh, pops, you don't need the more less. You know more music than what I do. He said, I wish I ever learned as much as you do. So finally, I start to fool around with the horn. I was going so fast with it by playing in the orchestra, drumming the orchestra. I know all them numbers that was playing, like all them old numbers. I know them. The tempo of them, I couldn't go wrong. It wasn't like a fella just had to pick up the instrument. So, I went on. So, one day they were short in the brass band. My brass band, my exhaustive brass band. So, Vic Gasper said, pop, you bring that old trombone and bring your brother on drum. I said, what one do you want? What one of my brothers? He said, well, any one you want, bring them. So, I used my older brother, Remus Manchin, because he was a good street drummer, first-class street drummer. So, I told him, I said, come on, bud. I used to call him buddy, come on, bud, make this money. I'm going to play trombone today. My first job out. I said, who told you that? I said, oh, man, Vic Gasper. He's going to be right there even to play in the barrow, huh? So, I knew all the marches and things, how they go. I knew all the marches and things, how they go and everything. I couldn't go wrong. I went on through so good. So, Harrison Barnes said, you know, I work in the D. We was living right across the street from each other and said, I work in the D. I mean, I can't get off. you gonna be the trombone player in the brass band. I said, okay, Harry, and use your brother on snare drums. I said, all right. We did that so often and so often. One day, we was playing the parade down on La Perue Street on a Sunday evening. I was playing the trombone at an armature on trumpet. And had old man, George Moret, on trumpet. And they said, we got to get another trumpet player. I said, why don't you try to dip him out? He said, man, he can't read. He said, well, he'll make out just like he'll make out. So I took my advice and said, we can't go out with no two trumpets because it's going to be all day parade. So I went on by Louis back there. Back then, I found Louis. I said, Louis, you gonna play in the brass band tomorrow? He said, oh, man, you know I can't make that. I can't make no brass band. I have a Dick Salsa band. You know that stuff. I said, we can play no music tomorrow. He ain't going to play. It's the only way you can get in through there and learn how to play that music. I said, all right. You there. I said, sure, I'm going to play trombone. I said, that's all right. I can play as much music in this corner as you can on the trombone. I know I can. That's Louis' turn. So got back down La Perru Street, back there by Muley's. Muley's wasn't running there, but another fellow was running there. That big jumbo bottle was a nickel. Louis took a big jumbo bottle and drank it down. He never did drink. And drank it down. Then he had the cramps. Had to lay Louis out. Louis got overheated and had the cramps for that jumbo bottle. He stayed right there. So we went and piddled on through with our, with our Louis. We went on through. So I made so good. At night I was coming to work right around the corner of you at the Muley and Willow. I was coming in to play with old man Humphrey. Willie Humphrey's daddy. Old man Humphrey. Is that Jim Humphrey?
